sections.title: Overview
sections.text: One of the tallest antelopes, with the largest horns in the bushbuck tribe (average ~120 cm).

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Eastern and southern Africa.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 120–315 kg; shoulder height 100–150 cm.

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: ~20.8–23 years recorded in captivity.

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: About 9 months (ADW range 7–8.7 months); seasonal breeder in southern Africa, calving when grass is high.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Male calves stay with the maternity herd 1.5–2 years; females longer. Adult males are often solitary or in bachelor groups.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Savanna/woodland and scrub forest with cover.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for specific Texas regions.

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Tropical/subtropical species; no verified cold-tolerance threshold was found. Provide windbreaks and shelter in freezes as a precaution.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Browser (leaves, shoots, pods) with some forbs.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: No verified species-specific protein % or mineral formula was found. Texas deer guidance (16–20% CP pellet; 13–16% CP for growth/reproduction) is sometimes used as a reference point but is not antelope-specific—work with a ruminant nutritionist/exotic vet.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Least Concern.

sections.title: Legal notes (general info, not legal advice)
sections.text: General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

sections.text: Large savanna antelope; males darken to black and develop large curved horns at about 3 years old.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: East and southern Africa savanna woodlands.

sections.title: Size

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Large oryx with straight ringed horns 60–150 cm long; introduced into Mexico and the southwestern US.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Southern Africa; wooded grassland at ~900–1,200 m elevation and arid areas.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: Females 180–225 kg, males 180–240 kg; shoulder height 115–125 cm; body length 180–195 cm.

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: ~18 years wild; 20–22 years captive.

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: ~8.5 months (270 days); calves 9–15 kg at birth; females mature at ~2 years.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Herding antelope; horns are used defensively.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Arid adapted: forage plus wild melons/cucumbers can supply all water needed (~3 L per 100 kg body weight daily).

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: INFERRED only: desert-adapted (see Habitat needs), so the arid Trans-Pecos/Chihuahuan Desert is the closest climate match; no Texas county distribution data found. See the interactive Texas species map (../site/map.html).

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Tallest land animal; needs specialist husbandry, especially for cold weather.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Sub-Saharan Africa.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: Bulls up to 1,930 kg, cows up to 1,180 kg; 4.7–5.7 m tall; calves 50–55 kg.

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 10–15 years wild; 20–25 years captive (record 27).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: ~457 days (range 400–468); females breed every 20–30 months; weaning 12–16 months.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Loose herds; females mature at 3–4 years, males breed from ~7 years.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Open savanna/woodland with browse.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Suitable anywhere in Texas only with a heated barn: AZA/USDA call for heated housing when temperatures average below 50 °F (inference: this occurs statewide in winter). See the interactive Texas species map (../site/map.html).

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: AZA: when average daily temperatures fall below 10 °C (50 °F), provide heated housing that holds at least 18 °C (65 °F), with areas near 24 °C (75 °F); measure at chest height of the smallest giraffe. USDA recommends keeping giraffes indoors in cold, inclement weather; a giraffe died in a drafty barn that was ~70°F up high but 45°F lower down. Acclimatized giraffes tolerate heat up to 49 °C (120 °F) with shade.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Follow the AZA Giraffe Care Manual for barrier and barn design; no ranch fence-height figure was verified for this page.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Browser; an adult male can eat up to 66 kg of food per day, surviving on ~7 kg in poor areas.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: Follow the AZA Giraffe Care Manual nutrition chapter; no protein % was verified for this page.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Cold stress/hypothermia is a major documented killer; once chilled, a giraffe struggles to regain body temperature without an outside heat source, and its immune system is compromised. Calves and juveniles are at greatest risk.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Vulnerable.

sections.title: Legal notes (general info, not legal advice)
sections.text: A USDA AWA exhibitor license is required if exhibited to the public. General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: One-humped domesticated camel, highly adapted to heat and water scarcity.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Domesticated; no wild population. Kept across North Africa, the Middle East and beyond.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 300–690 kg; males ~10% heavier than females (males 400–600 kg).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 40–50 years in captivity (max ~50).

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Hot, dry climates. Tolerates >30% water loss and can drink ~100 L in 10 minutes; body temperature varies daily from ~34 °C to 41 °C to save water.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: INFERRED only: desert-adapted (see Habitat needs), so the arid Trans-Pecos/Chihuahuan Desert is the closest climate match; no Texas county distribution data found. See the interactive Texas species map (../site/map.html).

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: Scottish DWA guidance (minimum, zoo/licence context): one camel ≥5×10 m; one male + two females ≥10×20 m. Pasture-kept animals need far more.

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Provide a shelter large enough for all animals, sited against the worst prevailing weather, plus shade through all daylight hours; lockable shelter recommended.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Wire mesh, visible high-tensile wire or post-and-rail at least 1.9 m (6 ft); mesh must not entangle heads or legs; barbed wire is not appropriate.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Not verified in detail for this page; consult the husbandry manual.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: No verified protein/mineral figures for this page.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: No verified species-specific list for this page; work with a camelid vet.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Not verified for this page; camels are large and can be dangerous—use experienced handlers.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Not assessed as a wild species (domesticated; no wild population).

sections.title: Legal notes (general info, not legal advice)
sections.text: Camels are listed under the UK Dangerous Wild Animals regime, a sign of handling risk; US state rules vary. General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Two-humped camel of Central Asian deserts with a heavy coat shed seasonally.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Central Asia (Gobi and steppe deserts); the wild Bactrian camel (C. ferus) is a separate, endangered species.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 300–690 kg; calves ~37 kg and mobile within 24 hours.

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: Average ~30 years wild (up to 50); ~35 years recorded in captivity.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Built for extreme seasonal desert temperatures: sheds its heavy coat with the seasons and tolerates a 6 °C rise in body temperature before sweating.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Coat and climate adaptation suggest better cold tolerance than dromedaries; no verified US region guidance found.

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: Scottish DWA guidance (minimum): one camel ≥5×10 m; one male + two females ≥10×20 m.

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Shelter for all animals sited against prevailing weather; lockable shelter recommended.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: At least 1.9 m (6 ft) mesh, visible high-tensile or post-and-rail; no barbed wire.

sections.text: Not verified in detail for this page.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: See native range and biology below.

sections.title: Native range

sections.title: Size

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 15–18 years typical in captivity; record 25+.

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: ~7 months (210 days); fall rut (Sept–Oct); single calf May–June.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Forest deer preferring dense understory; primarily nocturnal.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Documented free-ranging in major portions of Kerr, Bandera, Edwards and Real counties (Edwards Plateau/Hill Country). 1988 survey: confined on 207 ranches in 77 counties. See the interactive Texas species map (../site/map.html).

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: For supplementation TPWD recommends a 16–20% crude-protein pelleted feed rather than corn (corn is only 7–10% CP). AgriLife cites ~6–7% CP for rumen maintenance and 13–16% CP for growth, antler production and reproduction (white-tailed deer data; applied to exotic deer by analogy). Mineral program: set with a nutritionist/vet; no verified species figure.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Least Concern.

sections.title: Legal notes (general info, not legal advice)
sections.text: In Texas, exotic CWD-susceptible species (elk, red deer, sika and others) must carry official ID, have movements reported to TAHC within 48 hours, and eligible mortalities tested; TAHC ended its voluntary CWD Herd Certification Program on Sept 16, 2025. General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

AgriLife cites ~6–7% CP for rumen maintenance and 13–16% CP for growth, antler production and reproduction (white-tailed deer data; applied to exotic deer by analogy). Mineral program: set with a nutritionist/vet; no verified species figure.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Least Concern.

sections.title: Legal notes (general info, not legal advice)
sections.text: In Texas, exotic CWD-susceptible species (elk, red deer, sika and others) must carry official ID, have movements reported to TAHC within 48 hours, and eligible mortalities tested; TAHC ended its voluntary CWD Herd Certification Program on Sept 16, 2025. General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

sections.text: Banteng inhabit various areas in Southeast Asia. Believed to have first been domesticated on Java, they are also now found in Bali, Burma, Borneo, Thailand, and Malaysia.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Bontebok and blesbok are herbivores, they graze on grasses and herbage. Blesbok eat primarily red oat grass ( Themeda ), but also eat grasses in the genera Eragrostis and Chloromelas. Bontebok eat primarily grasses in the genera Bromus and Danthonia, however bontebok also feed on Eragrostis.….

sections.text: Historically, African buffalos were found throughout most of sub-Sahara Africa. Today their distribution is considerably reduced and in many areas largely limited to reserves.

sections.text: African buffalo can inhabit practically any habitat with permanent water and grass. sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Chinese Water Deer appears on the Exotic Wildlife Association species list as Chinese Water Deer — ESA: Not Listed; CITES: N/A.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: The Chinese water deer is found in the lower Yangtze Basin of east-central China and in Korea.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 12–18.5 kg (average 12.9 kg) (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 12 years (wild, average); 11.5 years (captivity, average).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: offspring per birth: 6.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Chinese water deer live among tall reeds, rushes along rivers, and in tall grass on mountains and cultivated fields. ADW biomes: savanna or grassland, forest.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: The diet of the Chinese water deer includes reeds, coarse grasses, vegetables, and beets. The Chinese water deer has a four chambered stomach, but the rumen pillars are poorly developed.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: For supplementation TPWD recommends a 16–20% crude-protein pelleted feed rather than corn (corn is only 7–10% CP). AgriLife cites ~6–7% CP for rumen maintenance and 13–16% CP for growth, antler production and reproduction (white-tailed deer data; applied to exotic deer by analogy). Mineral program: set with a nutritionist/vet; no verified species figure.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Vulnerable.

sections.text: General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Hog Deer appears on the Exotic Wildlife Association species list as Hog Deer — ESA: Not Listed; CITES: Appendix I.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Axis porcinus has a native geographic range throughout India, including the Himalayan foothill zone and Southeast Asia, including Burma and Thailand.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 36–50 kg (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 20 years (wild, average); 20 years (captivity, average); 10 years (wild, average).

sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Hog deer feed nocturnally. They both graze and browse, but seem to prefer grazing. ADW diet type: herbivore, folivore.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: For supplementation TPWD recommends a 16–20% crude-protein pelleted feed rather than corn (corn is only 7–10% CP). AgriLife cites ~6–7% CP for rumen maintenance and 13–16% CP for growth, antler production and reproduction (white-tailed deer data; applied to exotic deer by analogy). Mineral program: set with a nutritionist/vet; no verified species figure.

sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.text: Kob are herbivorous. They eat grasses and reeds, and may migrate great distances to graze along watercourses.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Mule Deer appears on the Exotic Wildlife Association species list as Mule Deer — ESA: Not Listed; CITES: N/A.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Odocoileus hemionus occurs over most of North America west of the 100th meridian from 23 degrees to 60 degrees N. The eastern edge of the usual range extends from southwestern Saskatchewan through central North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and western Texas.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 43–150 kg (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 22 years (captivity, average).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: Gestation average 207 days; offspring per birth: 1.5.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Odocoileus hemionus is remarkably adaptable. Of at least sixty types of natural vegetation west of the 100th meridian in the United States, all but two or three are or once were occupied by O. hemionus. Several additional vegetation types are inhabited in Canada and Mexico as well. ADW biomes: desert or dune, savanna or grassland, chaparral, forest, mountains.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Odocoileus hemionus occurs over most of North America west of the 100th meridian from 23 degrees to 60 degrees N. The eastern edge of the usual range extends from southwestern Saskatchewan through central North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Kansas, and western Texas.

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: For supplementation TPWD recommends a 16–20% crude-protein pelleted feed rather than corn (corn is only 7–10% CP). AgriLife cites ~6–7% CP for rumen maintenance and 13–16% CP for growth, antler production and reproduction (white-tailed deer data; applied to exotic deer by analogy). Mineral program: set with a nutritionist/vet; no verified species figure.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Least Concern.

sections.title: Legal notes (general info, not legal advice)
sections.text: Native Texas deer: holding white-tailed or mule deer in captivity requires a TPWD permit (deer breeder program), and CWD movement/testing rules apply. General information, not legal advice. USDA APHIS licensing under the Animal Welfare Act applies to dealers and exhibitors; check USDA and your state wildlife and animal-health agencies before buying, moving or selling.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Reeves's Muntjac appears on the Exotic Wildlife Association species list as Muntjac — ESA: Not Listed; CITES: Appendix III.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Muntiacus reevesi has a native range that extends throughout the subtropical forests of southeastern China and Taiwan.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 11–28 kg (average 18 kg) (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 18 years (captivity, range); 10-12 years (wild, average); 23.2 years (captivity, average).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: Gestation 6.97–7.33 months; average 7 months; offspring per birth: 1–2.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Muntiacus reevesi is a forest creature in its native country of China. It creates paths through the subtropical rainforests at moderate elevations, which is why it has been termed by some as a bush hugger. ADW biomes: forest, rainforest, scrub forest.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Like most deer, Javan rusa eat primarily grass and leaves. They hardly drink any water because they get their fluid from the grass and the leaves. ADW diet type: herbivore, folivore.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: For supplementation TPWD recommends a 16–20% crude-protein pelleted feed rather than corn (corn is only 7–10% CP). AgriLife cites ~6–7% CP for rumen maintenance and 13–16% CP for growth, antler production and reproduction (white-tailed deer data; applied to exotic deer by analogy). Mineral program: set with a nutritionist/vet; no verified species figure.

sections.text: Springbok range includes south and southwestern Africa, mainly in the countries of Namibia, Botswana, Angola and the Republic of South Africa.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 33–46 kg (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 19 years (captivity, average); 20 years (wild, average).

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.text: Springboks are mostly confined to game reserves and farms in treeless savanna associated with the edges of dry lake beds. ADW biomes: savanna or grassland.

sections.title: Where they thrive (Texas / US)
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Space per animal
sections.text: No verified species-specific stocking rate was found. Carrying capacity depends on rainfall, range condition and competing grazers—get a range/stocking assessment (NRCS or Texas A&M AgriLife).

sections.title: Housing & shelter
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Fencing
sections.text: Texas Parks & Wildlife states game fences at least 8 ft high (woven-wire or high-tensile) are the only fully reliable deer-exclusion fence. That is the common high-fence standard for deer and antelope; a species-specific minimum for this animal was not found in a primary source.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: The springbok is an intermediate browser, using both grass and browse. The shift from one food source to the other takes place seasonally.

sections.title: Feed & supplementation
sections.text: No verified species-specific protein % or mineral formula was found. Texas deer guidance (16–20% CP pellet; 13–16% CP for growth/reproduction) is sometimes used as a reference point but is not antelope-specific—work with a ruminant nutritionist/exotic vet.

sections.title: Common health issues & parasites
sections.text: Haemonchus contortus and Longistrongylus dominate abomasal worm burdens in free-ranging exotic antelope in Texas (sable, addax, blesbok studied); captive wild ruminants show anthelmintic resistance, so use fecal egg counts and fecal egg-count reduction tests instead of routine blanket deworming.

sections.title: Vet care & vaccination
sections.text: No vaccines are labeled for this species in the US; any vaccination protocol is extra-label and should be set by a veterinarian experienced with exotic hoofstock. (No specific protocol was verified for this page.)

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Conservation status
sections.text: IUCN Red List: Least Concern.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Senegal Bushbaby (Northern Lesser Galago) appears on the Exotic Wildlife Association species list as Bushbaby — ESA: Not Listed; CITES: Appendix II.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Bush babies occupy the forested and bush regions of Africa south of the Sahara. Their range also extends to some nearby islands, including Zanzibar.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 0.095–0.3 kg (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 10 years (captivity, average); 3 to 4 years (wild, typical); 10 years (captivity, typical).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: Gestation 110–120 days; offspring per birth: 1–3.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Lesser bush babies are well-adapted to living in drier areas. They generally occupy the the savannah woodlands south of the Sahara and are excluded only from the southern tip of Africa. ADW biomes: forest, rainforest, scrub forest.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Alpaca appears on the Exotic Wildlife Association species list as Alpaca — ESA: Not Listed; CITES: N/A.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: The native range of Lama pacos includes the central and southern Andes from Peru to Argentina at elevations of up to 4800 meters.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 55–65 kg (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 20 years (captivity, average); 5 to 10 years (wild, typical); 25.8 years (captivity, average).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: Gestation 242–345 days; average 190.5 days; offspring per birth: 1; females mature at 12 to 15 months.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: Alpacas inhabit the Andean Altiplano, i.e. the Andean high plateau, preferably near wet areas. ADW biomes: savanna or grassland, mountains. Elevation range 1000–4800 m.

sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Natural diet
sections.text: Lama pacos is a strict grazer. In a highland region of Chile, Castellano et al. reported that the alpaca diet was dominated by grasses such as Festuca nardifolia, Deschampsia caespitosa, and Agrostis tolucensis, cushion plants Oxychloe andina, bunch grasses Festuca orthophylla, and the woody shrub…. ADW diet type: herbivore, folivore.

sections.title: Handling & capture
sections.text: Capture myopathy—muscle damage from pursuit, restraint and transport—is often fatal in wild ungulates. Minimize chase time and stress, avoid hot conditions, use appropriate chemical immobilization by a vet, and release/unload quickly.

sections.title: Overview
sections.text: Llama appears on the Exotic Wildlife Association species list as Llama — ESA: Not Listed; CITES: N/A.

sections.title: Native range
sections.text: Llamas have a native range all along the Andes mountains, but are not found in the wild. Lama glama can be found commercially throughout North America, Europe and Australia.

sections.title: Size
sections.text: 130–155 kg (average 140 kg) (ADW range).

sections.title: Lifespan
sections.text: 10 to 20 years (captivity, range); 16 years (captivity, average); 10 to 20 years (captivity, typical).

sections.title: Breeding & gestation
sections.text: Gestation 10–12 months; offspring per birth: 0–1; females mature at 2 to 3 years.

sections.title: Temperament & social structure
sections.text: Not verified from a primary source for this page.

sections.title: Habitat needs
sections.text: The Andean highlands, especially the Altiplano of southeast Peru and western Bolivia, is the natural habitat of L. glama. These plateaus are covered with low growth, including various shrubs stunted trees and grasses. ADW biomes: mountains. Elevation range 2300–4000 m.

sections.text: Llamas browse on low shrubs, lichens, and mountain vegetation. Llamas make use of native shrubs and grasses including Parastrephia sp., Baccharis sp. (shrubs) as well as Munroa sp., Eragrostis sp., and Triseobromus sp. (grasses). ADW diet type: herbivore, folivore.
